meta.title: Linux EEVDF scheduler: virtual lag, eligibility, virtual deadlines
meta.subject: Computer science
meta.topic: EEVDF (Earliest Eligible Virtual Deadline First) in Linux

story.title: How Linux 6.6 lets short turns jump the line, without extra CPU

tldr: Linux 6.6 replaced CFS's "smallest vruntime" rule and its pile of latency heuristics with two checks. A task is eligible only if it is not ahead of the weighted average, and among eligible tasks the one with the earliest virtual deadline runs. Each request's size sets its deadline, so latency is chosen per task while long-run share is still set by weight.
why: Why it matters: every mainline kernel from 6.6 on runs it, and it is the source of most latency tuning questions and kernel-upgrade regressions in CPU-bound services.

cards.title: A fair barista who lets short turns jump the line
cards.brief:
Everyone gets an equal share of the barista's day. EEVDF keeps a ledger of who is owed time, and gives each customer a finish-by time that is earlier for shorter turns.

Short turns are served sooner, while total time over the day stays equal.

cards.title: Six things to know first
cards.brief:
• Runqueue: the per-CPU list of runnable tasks.
  • Weight: nice 0 is 1024; each nice step is about 1.25×.
  • vruntime: CPU time scaled by 1024/w, so heavy tasks age slower.
  • Red-black tree of runnable entities; cgroups nest them.

cards.title: Every mainline kernel since 6.6 runs it, mostly unseen
cards.brief: Default on Ubuntu 24.04, Debian 13, Fedora and Arch, on Android GKI 6.6+, and in containers through cpu.weight. Knobs: nice, a per-thread custom slice (6.12+), and sched_ext for whole custom policies.

cards.title: "Earliest virtual deadline among the eligible" hides five things
cards.brief: The slogan hides what the "virtual" clock is, how eligibility is tested, what sleep does to lag, that slice and weight are orthogonal, and that the decision covers one runqueue only.

cards.title: CFS let sleepers jump the queue, and each tuning knob broke another
cards.brief: CFS placed a waking task near the minimum vruntime, so it won at once. Latency came from tunables in mixed units that fought each other. Needed: a bounded fairness error, a latency request independent of weight, and fewer magic numbers.

cards.title: A bank ledger with a stopwatch: lag is the balance, deadline the due date
cards.brief: Lag is your balance with the CPU, and positive means it owes you. Only non-negative accounts get served. The catch: the reference point is a weighted mean that moves whenever tasks join, leave or reweight.

cards.title: Eligibility and deadlines pick every millisecond
cards.brief:
Three equal-weight tasks ask for 3 ms, 3 ms and 1 ms slices. Over 24 ms each gets 8 ms, the same as the others. The eligibility check and the deadline order decide every millisecond.

Step-through trace inside.

cards.title: Lag stays within one request of the ideal share
cards.brief: The bound is −c < lag < max(cmax, q), where c is the request size and q the quantum. Lags sum to zero because V is the weighted mean. A joining task's saved lag is inflated by (W+w)/W.

cards.title: Eligibility bounds unfairness; deadlines let each task choose its latency
cards.brief: Remove eligibility and tiny-slice tasks starve the rest. Remove deadlines and you get CFS, fair with no latency control. Remove lag memory and one sleep wipes out a debt. Each piece covers a different failure.

cards.title: Slice sets when a task runs, weight sets how much
cards.brief:
Slice and weight are orthogonal. Custom slices run from 100 µs to 100 ms. Alternatives are CFS-style heuristics, SCHED_DEADLINE reservations and BPF sched_ext.

Slice and weight simulator inside.

cards.title: A 2024 overflow turned a weight change into a NULL dereference
cards.brief: CVE-2024-35985 made every entity look ineligible, so the picker returned NULL. Tick granularity, per-CPU-only fairness and cgroup reweighting also bite, and "short slice = more CPU" is a myth.

cards.title: Linux adds clamped lag, parity protection and delayed dequeue to the paper
cards.brief: RUN_TO_PARITY protects the running task. Delayed dequeue (6.12) stops sleep-based lag gaming. Cgroups each get their own EEVDF, and an augmented tree prunes subtrees with no eligible task. The 1995 paper has none of these.

cards.title: Policy moved into BPF and LLM-written schedulers
cards.brief: Once fairness and latency were settled per runqueue, the work moved to policy (sched_ext, synthesised schedulers), locality hints and proxy execution for priority inversion. SchedCP claims 1.79× on a kernel build, unreplicated.

cards.title: Latency SLOs, global fairness and heterogeneous cores are still open
cards.brief: Slices are the only latency handle, and per-runqueue bounds don't compose into a global one under a periodic balancer. Cgroup reweighting and asymmetric cores are unsolved. LLM-written BPF schedulers are checked for memory safety, not fairness.

cards.title: From GPS (1993) through CFS (2007) to EEVDF in Linux (2023)
cards.brief: GPS (1993) → WFQ and WF2Q → stride scheduling and the EEVDF paper (1995) → CFS (Linux 2.6.23, 2007) → EEVDF in Linux 6.6 (2023) → custom slices and sched_ext (6.12).

cards.title: A 30-second simulator shows equal shares despite unequal slices
cards.brief: python3 eevdf_sim.py reproduces the 8/8/8 trace. Shrink C's slice, or delete the eligibility filter and watch C monopolise. On Linux ≥ 6.12, try NO_RUN_TO_PARITY and compare perf sched latency.

cards.title: Test yourself
cards.brief: 22 questions from mechanism to open research. Reveal, then mark ✓ or ✗; marks feed your progress ring.

cards.title: Three follow-ups: PELT, sched_ext, SCHED_DEADLINE
cards.brief: PELT and load balancing, sched_ext with BPF schedulers, and SCHED_DEADLINE's CBS admission control. These are the parts EEVDF does not cover.

cards.title: Papers, kernel source and articles, plus unverified claims
cards.brief: The 1995 paper, kernel source and docs, LWN and Phoronix, seven arXiv entries, and a list of claims I could not verify.

cold.q: What is the default slice on a machine with 8 or more CPUs?
cold.reveal: On 8 or more CPUs it is 2.8 ms. The base is 0.7 ms, multiplied by 1 + the rounded-down log2 of the CPU count, with the count capped at 8. Many distro docs just say 3 ms, from an older constant.

mech.q: Three equal-weight tasks run for 24 ms. A and B ask for 3 ms turns, C asks for 1 ms. How much CPU does C get?
options: The same as A and B: 8 ms each
mech.reveal: 8 ms, the same as A and B. The eligibility check forces everyone back to the average, so the short slice changes when C runs, not how much it gets.

knobs.q: A thread asks for a custom slice of 1 µs. What range does the kernel clamp it into?
knobs.reveal: 100 µs to 100 ms. The kernel clamps sched_runtime into that range (Linux 6.12 and later). Shorter requests are raised to 100 µs.

breaks.q: Which kernel release fixed the CVE-2024-35985 overflow?
breaks.reveal: 6.9, fixed in 6.9-rc6 (commit 1560d1f6eb6b) and backported. An s64 multiply overflowed, so every task looked ineligible, and pick_eevdf() returned NULL.

questions.q: Walk pick_eevdf() when the leftmost-by-deadline node is ineligible. Which subtree does it descend?
questions.a: Loop: go to the left child while the left subtree's min_vruntime is eligible, because an eligible task with an earlier deadline exists there. Otherwise test the current node, and otherwise go right. The first eligible node found is the earliest-deadline eligible task.

questions.q: What does update_deadline() do, and when?
questions.a: When v ≥ vd, the request is used up. It sets vd = v + slice·1024/w and requests a reschedule.

questions.q: Why does the kernel compare avg ≥ key·load rather than avg/load ≥ key?
questions.a: Division truncates and loses precision, while cross-multiplication is exact. The cost is a 128-bit product or overflow checks.

questions.q: What does place_entity() multiply lag by, and why (W+w)/W?
questions.a: It multiplies by (W+w)/W because adding the task pulls V toward its own vruntime and shrinks its apparent lag by W/(W+w). Inflating the lag pre-compensates; the derivation is in the math card.

questions.q: What state does a sched_delayed task hold?
questions.a: Its clamped (≤ 0) vlag and its deadline. It stays on the tree, ineligible, aging in virtual time until it is picked or woken.

questions.q: Why must V be the weighted average?
questions.a: So that Σ lag<sub>i</sub> = 0 (conservation), and V is the fluid-model reference: each task should have received w<sub>i</sub>·ΔV.

questions.q: Why is the tree keyed on deadline but augmented with min_vruntime?
questions.a: Deadline order gives the answer among the eligible. min_vruntime lets whole subtrees with no eligible task be pruned, so the pick is O(log n).

questions.q: Why is lag stored as virtual lag?
questions.a: Because lag = w·vlag, and vlag does not depend on weight. A reweight becomes one scaling, and comparisons avoid multiplying by w.

questions.q: Why do deadlines use slice/weight?
questions.a: The same request costs less virtual time at higher weight. Heavier tasks therefore get earlier deadlines and more CPU per unit of V.

questions.q: Remove eligibility: what pathological workload appears?
questions.a: A flood of tiny-slice tasks always holds the earliest deadline and starves the long-slice tasks. Lag is unbounded.

questions.q: Every slice is 0.1 ms: what happens to throughput and fairness?
questions.a: Context-switch and cache costs rise sharply, throughput drops, and the fairness error shrinks to about one slice.

questions.q: PLACE_LAG is off: describe an exploit.
questions.a: Sleep briefly each slice and wake. The negative lag is discarded, so you re-enter near V and never pay back the overconsumption.

questions.q: A task's weight doubles while it is queued: what must be rescaled?
questions.a: Its vruntime, vlag and deadline must be rescaled (the reweight path), with the same lag clamp. Without the clamp the arithmetic can overflow, as in CVE-2024-35985.

questions.q: How can a task game EEVDF through sleeping, and which feature closes that?
questions.a: Short sleeps reset its negative lag. DELAY_DEQUEUE keeps such a task queued and ineligible, so it burns off its lag instead.

questions.q: How can unprivileged code shorten its slice to hurt others, and what bounds the damage?
questions.a: A short sched_runtime makes the task preempt-prone with early deadlines. Eligibility caps its share at its weight, so the damage is extra context switches, not extra CPU.

questions.q: How did CVE-2024-35985 turn a weight change into a kernel NULL dereference?
questions.a: reweight_eevdf() computed vlag without the clamp. Weight is 20-bit fixed point, so the s64 product overflowed. entity_eligible() then returned false for every task, and pick_eevdf() returned NULL.

questions.q: How does EEVDF relate to WF2Q, and why does the eligibility test match?
questions.a: Both use the same eligibility gate, start time ≤ virtual time. WF2Q uses it to cap how far ahead of GPS a flow can run, and EEVDF uses it to bound lag.

questions.q: How does cpu.weight interact with hierarchical group entities?
questions.a: Each group has a scheduling entity per CPU, weighted from cpu.weight. It competes in its parent's EEVDF, while its inner tasks run their own EEVDF. h_load carries the effective weight.

questions.q: How is SCHED_DEADLINE different from a virtual deadline?
questions.a: SCHED_DEADLINE uses wall-clock runtime, deadline and period, with admission control and CBS. EEVDF's deadlines are virtual, relative to a fair-share reference, and carry no guarantee.

questions.q: Can per-runqueue lag bounds compose into a global fairness bound with a periodic balancer?
questions.a: Open. The balancer equalises load rather than lag, and it runs on timescales much longer than a slice.

questions.q: What would a latency-SLO interface look like, instead of a slice?
questions.a: Open. Candidates include latency-nice, SLO hints passed through sched_ext maps, and proxy-execution-aware slices.

questions.q: How should lag be defined across heterogeneous cores?
questions.a: Open. Capacity-scaling vruntime, as PELT does for utilisation, is the obvious approach but unsettled.
